passage: I sit behind Jeevan in class, so I saw everything. On Tuesday Anirban walked over before the bell and put a small paper packet of painted pebbles on Jeevan's desk. He didn't say much, just stood there smiling. Jeevan looked at the packet, then at the floor, and said, "Thank you, but I don't want to take this. No, thank you." Anirban nodded slowly and went back to his seat, though he kept glancing over during maths. Jeevan tucked the packet into the corner of the desk and kept both hands on the notebook. At lunch Jeevan stopped by the teacher's table and said a few words I couldn't hear. I can't tell what Jeevan felt inside, but the voice stayed steady.

qa.q: What did Anirban put on Jeevan's desk?
qa.a: A small paper packet of painted pebbles.

qa.q: What might Jeevan have been feeling when saying no, thank you, and what in the passage points to it?
qa.a: Jeevan may have felt unsure but firm, since the voice stayed steady; the narrator admits they can't tell what Jeevan felt inside for sure.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do if Anirban keeps glancing over and starts to push?
qa.a: Jeevan could repeat the polite no, thank you, and tell the teacher or another trusted adult if it continues.

qa.q: How might Anirban see that moment?
qa.a: He may feel a little embarrassed or disappointed, which could be why he nodded slowly and kept glancing over. Still, the kind and clear answer let him go back to his seat without a scene.

grounding: A boy gives a small gift and keeps looking, and the child politely and clearly says no, thank you, seen by a classmate.

passage: During the free period in the school library, Vishal leaned over the atlas and whispered, "Promise you won't tell? I'm scared I'll fail the reading test and I don't want anyone to know." Rajni felt a warm flutter; out of everyone, he had picked her. She promised. When Kabir waved from the next table and asked what they were whispering about, Rajni just shrugged and said, "Just a boring map thing." Her shoulders felt heavy afterwards, as if she were carrying a full glass of water. That evening she decided that if Vishal ever seemed truly hurt or in trouble, she would tell the class teacher and explain why. For now, keeping his words safe felt like her job.

qa.q: Where were Rajni and Vishal when he whispered his secret?
qa.a: They were in the school library during the free period, leaning over an atlas.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel about being chosen to hear the secret?
qa.a: Special and responsible: she felt a warm flutter because he had picked her, and afterwards her shoulders felt heavy like she was carrying a full glass of water.

qa.q: What should Rajni do if Vishal's secret ever means he could be hurt?
qa.a: She should tell the class teacher, a trusted adult, and explain to Vishal why she is doing it. 🙂

qa.q: How might Kabir see Rajni's shrug?
qa.a: Kabir only heard about a boring map thing, so he probably sees nothing unusual and does not learn Vishal's secret.

grounding: A friend shares a secret and the child feels special and responsible, keeps it, and plans to tell a trusted adult only if someone could be hurt.

passage: Come, Vinita, sit. Old Rafiq was ten once, and I nearly made a big mistake. My friend Salim whispered that his sister's wedding had been called off, and no neighbour knew yet. Oh, that secret sat on my tongue like hot jalebi! I wanted to tell just one person, my cousin Aslam. I walked to his gate twice. Then I thought, trust is like a glass bangle; drop it once and no glue can mend it. So I went home and drank water instead. Years later Salim told me he had never worried, because I was the one who kept my word. And if I had slipped, I would have gone to him that same evening and said sorry.

qa.q: What secret did Salim whisper to Rafiq?
qa.a: That his sister's wedding had been called off, and no neighbour knew yet.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling as he walked to Aslam's gate twice?
qa.a: A strong itch to tell, since the secret sat on his tongue like hot jalebi, but he also held back and thought about how fragile trust is.

qa.q: What would Rafiq have done if he had slipped and told Aslam?
qa.a: He would have gone to Salim that same evening, owned up and said sorry.

qa.q: How might Salim have felt about Rafiq keeping his word?
qa.a: Salim says he never worried, so he likely felt safe and trusting with Rafiq.

grounding: A child is tempted to pass on a juicy secret, reminds himself that trust is fragile, keeps it, and says he would have owned up and apologised if he had slipped.

passage: On the walk to the tram stop in Lisbon, Javier called out, "Night-light Rafael!" and two other boys laughed. Rafael's ears burned. Only Marisol knew he still slept with a small lamp on. He had told her in Year Five, and she had sworn on her bracelet. He said nothing all the way home, chewing his lip, and threw his bag on the bed hard. Next morning he found Marisol by the lockers. "You told," he said, voice low. "It felt awful, like everyone was looking inside my room." Marisol's face went red. He did not shout, and he did not spread her secrets. He only said he needed some time before telling her anything else.

qa.q: What did Javier call out to Rafael?
qa.a: He called out "Night-light Rafael!"

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when he stayed silent on the way home, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Hurt and hot with embarrassment: his ears burned, he chewed his lip and threw his bag on the bed hard.

qa.q: What would you advise Rafael about trusting Marisol from now on?
qa.a: It is fine to be careful and share only small things for a while, but not to get back at her by spreading her secrets.

qa.q: What might Marisol be feeling when Rafael says "You told"?
qa.a: Her face went red, so she is probably ashamed and worried, and she may want to explain or say sorry.

grounding: A child's secret told to a best friend is now known by everyone; he feels hot and hurt, says how it felt, and becomes careful without being cruel back.

passage: Sangeeta, you asked how I knew to speak up for your friend. Let me tell you about when I was eleven. I am Lakshmi, remember. My friend Padma whispered in the school yard that someone at her home hurt her when they were angry, and that I must never tell. I couldn't eat that night. It was too heavy for one girl to hold. Next day I told Padma gently, "I care about you too much to carry this alone. Telling our teacher isn't betraying you; it's helping." She cried, but she came with me. The teacher listened calmly and made sure Padma reached grown-ups who knew what to do.

qa.q: How old was Lakshmi when Padma told her the secret?
qa.a: Lakshmi was eleven.

qa.q: What was weighing on Lakshmi that night, and why?
qa.a: The secret was too heavy for one girl to hold, and she was worried for Padma and did not know what to do, which is why she couldn't eat.

qa.q: How could a child explain to a hurting friend why they must tell a teacher?
qa.a: They can say gently that telling isn't betraying but helping, and that they care too much to carry it alone.

qa.q: How might Padma have felt when Lakshmi said she would tell the teacher?
qa.a: Scared and upset, since she cried and had asked for silence, but she came along, which shows she trusted Lakshmi.

grounding: A friend says she is being hurt at home; the child finds it too big to carry alone and gently explains that telling a teacher is loving, not disloyal.

passage:
Monday. During a quarrel over the cricket score, Vijay shouted, "At least I don't cry in the toilets when I miss the choir!" Sarita's mouth fell open. The whole line of children heard.

Tuesday. Vijay's dal sat untouched. First he practised saying, "You made me so angry," then stopped. She had not made him say it. His stomach twisted.

Thursday. He found Sarita by the water tank. "I'm sorry I told everyone your secret. It was mine to keep, and I broke it. No excuses." Sarita looked at her shoes. "I'm still upset," she said. "I don't know when I'll feel okay." Vijay nodded. "That's fair. I'll wait."

qa.q: What did Vijay shout during the quarrel over the cricket score?
qa.a: He shouted, "At least I don't cry in the toilets when I miss the choir!"

qa.q: What did Vijay realise on Tuesday about blaming Sarita?
qa.a: He realised she had not made him say it, so the blame was his own, and this made his stomach twist.

qa.q: What would you advise Vijay to do after Sarita says she is still upset?
qa.a: Give her time without pressing, and show through steady small actions that he can be trusted again.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sarita on Thursday at the water tank?
qa.a: She is probably still hurt and embarrassed because the whole line heard, so she needs time even though the sorry was honest.

grounding: A child lets out a friend's secret in a fight, feels awful, apologises without excuses and accepts that trust may take time.

passage:
"Mama, can I sit with you?" Nandini asked, twisting the end of her dupatta.
"Of course. What's on your mind?" Sunaina put down the peas.
"There's something I have to say. Promise not to shout?"
"I'll listen first. Then we'll think together."
"Miss wrote a note in my diary three days ago. I hid it under my mattress. I broke Rhea's glasses in the playground by accident, and I was scared you'd be so angry."
"Oh, Nandini. Thank you for telling me." Sunaina took a slow breath. "I don't love that it was hidden, but I'm glad you came. Let's read the note together. 🙂"
"You're not angry?"
"A little worried. Not angry at you for telling me."

qa.q: Where did Nandini hide the teacher's note?
qa.a: She hid it under her mattress.

qa.q: What was Nandini worried about before she spoke up?
qa.a: She was scared her mother would be so angry about Rhea's broken glasses, which is why she twisted her dupatta and asked for a promise not to shout.

qa.q: How can Sunaina keep talking about this feel safe for Nandini?
qa.a: She can stay calm, listen first and read the note together, as she does, so telling her feels safe. 🙂

qa.q: How might Sunaina be feeling as Nandini talks?
qa.a: A little worried but glad that Nandini came, since she took a slow breath and thanked her.

grounding: A child hides a worry from her parents for fear of anger, then opens with a request not to shout and meets a calm parent.

passage:
Monday. Mahima leaned over the desk. "Tell me what Tanvi told you about her brother and I'll be your best friend forever." Deepak's stomach dipped. He had eaten lunch alone all week. "No," he said, and looked at his pencil box.

Wednesday. She was waiting by the water cooler. "Last chance. Otherwise nobody sits with you." Deepak's hands felt cold, but he said, "That's not being friends. I'm not telling," and walked to the library.

Friday. Mahima blocked the corridor again, whispering the same demand. This time Deepak went straight to the class teacher and told everything, even the part where he had almost said yes. The teacher thanked him and said they would talk to Mahima.

qa.q: What did Mahima want Deepak to tell her?
qa.a: She wanted to know what Tanvi told him about her brother.

qa.q: Why might Deepak have felt tempted on Monday even though he said no?
qa.a: He had eaten lunch alone all week, so the offer of a best friend was tempting, though he still said no.

qa.q: What did Deepak's choice on Friday accomplish?
qa.a: Telling the class teacher moved the pressure from him to an adult who could talk to Mahima, so he did not have to handle it alone.

qa.q: How might Tanvi feel if she learned what happened?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and grateful that her secret stayed safe, though she may not know how close it came.

grounding: A classmate offers friendship only in exchange for someone's secret; the child says no, walks away and finally tells an adult when she keeps pressing.

passage: Anjali, come sit by me. I am Elizabeth, and I'm going to tell you something I wish someone had told me at ten. A grown-up who visited our street once said, "This is our secret. Don't tell your parents." My stomach went tight and cold, and I wanted to run. For two days I said nothing, thinking I had done something wrong. Then I whispered it to my mother in the kitchen. She hugged me and said, "None of this is your fault, and telling me was brave." She spoke to people who could keep me safe. Any secret that makes you uneasy, my dear, you bring to a trusted grown-up. Always.

qa.q: How long did Elizabeth stay silent before telling her mother?
qa.a: She said nothing for two days.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth stay silent for two days?
qa.a: She thought she had done something wrong, and her stomach went tight and cold, so she was afraid.

qa.q: What should Anjali do if a grown-up ever says "This is our secret. Don't tell your parents"?
qa.a: Anjali should tell a trusted grown-up, because any secret that makes them uneasy is one to share.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's mother have felt hearing the whisper?
qa.a: Probably worried and protective, since she hugged Elizabeth, said it was not her fault and spoke to people who could keep her safe.

grounding: An elder recalls an older person saying this is our secret, and how telling her mother was brave, right and never her fault.

passage: After choir practice the music room emptied, and Aadhya stayed behind, tightening her shoelaces for no reason. "Ira, can I tell you something? My parents are moving apart, and Papa is getting his own flat." Her voice cracked. Ira didn't gasp or ask a hundred questions. She sat on the piano bench, patted the space beside her, and just listened. Days later Aadhya overheard Kavya asking why she had been so quiet. Ira said only, "She'll tell you if she wants." Aadhya's chest felt lighter. She slipped a packet of mango candy into Ira's bag with a note: "Thanks for keeping it safe."

qa.q: Where did Aadhya tell Ira her private news?
qa.a: In the music room, after choir practice.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel after Ira listened and kept it private, and what shows it?
qa.a: Lighter and closer to Ira: her chest felt lighter and she left mango candy and a thank-you note. 🤍

qa.q: How could Aadhya keep repaying Ira's trust?
qa.a: By keeping Ira's private things as safely as Ira kept hers, and by showing up quietly for her in small ways.

qa.q: How might Kavya have felt about Ira's answer?
qa.a: Kavya may feel a little left out, but Ira's words also show that Aadhya will not be pushed to tell.

grounding: A child tells a friend something private, the friend just listens and keeps it, and the child feels lighter and closer.
